title: Reflections on Anger and Control in the Workplace: July 10, 2022
content: On July 10, 2022, at 10:47 PM, the user reflected on a troubling incident that occurred the previous day, July 9, 2022. They had lost their temper over a spreadsheet formatting issue when Xiao Wang reversed the order of data columns. In front of their colleagues, the user expressed their frustration with harsh words, noticing Xiao Wang's face go pale but continuing to emphasize the importance of details in product quality and the company's survival. The user questioned their own anger, realizing it stemmed from a deeper issue of setting stricter standards and perhaps trying to prove or control something in their life. They mentioned a conversation with Li Meifang, who had asked about their well-being, but the user chose not to respond, indicating a pattern of withdrawal. They also reflected on their May medical report, which advised them to 'pay attention' to their changing body and the passage of time. The user reorganized tools in the workshop and recorded their purposes, aware that their colleagues, Chen Hao and Chen Yu, would not use them. They expressed concern about their ability to continue in their job and mentioned an upcoming chess game with friends, feeling increasingly disconnected and quiet. The user acknowledged their need for control and the fear they instilled in their subordinates, believing it made them diligent. They concluded by sharing with Meifang over dinner that another formatting error had occurred that day, reinforcing their belief in the necessity of strict standards and documentation, despite knowing their subordinates were afraid of them. Meifang advised them not to push too hard, but the user felt a constant urge to hurry, wanting to accomplish everything while they still could.

original_messages.content:
July 10, 2022, 10:47 PM

I pulled out this unused notebook, though I’m not sure why. Maybe it’s because what happened yesterday is still spinning in my head.

I lost my temper yesterday over a spreadsheet formatting issue. Xiao Wang had reversed the order of the data columns, and I pointed it out in front of everyone, using some pretty harsh words. His face went pale instantly. I saw it, but I didn’t stop. Instead, I kept going on and on about how "details determine product quality, and product quality determines the company's survival."

Thinking back now, what was I so angry about? A formatting error. It was that simple.

But it wasn’t, really.

I’ve noticed myself setting stricter standards lately. Stricter inspection processes. Stricter requirements. As if doing this could... could what? I can’t quite put my finger on it. Maybe I’m trying to prove something. Maybe I’m trying to control something.

Li Meifang asked me what was wrong last night, but I didn't answer. She’s long since used to it.

I’ve gone over my May medical report three times now. The doctor said there’s nothing majorly wrong, just that I need to "pay attention." Pay attention to what? Pay attention to time passing. Pay attention to my body changing. Pay attention to how many more years I can keep doing this job.

I reorganized the tools in the workshop again recently. I’m recording the purpose of each one, one by one. Chen Hao won’t use them. Neither will Chen Yu. They have their own lives. I know this, yet I’m still taking notes. Why? While I can still move?

How many years of movement do I have left?

I’m supposed to play chess with my friends next week. I don’t know what to say to them. Lately, when I’m with them, I’ve been pathetically quiet. I was always a man of few words, but now I feel like I can’t even focus on the game. My mind is always elsewhere.

I’m trying to fight something off by exerting more control. I know this. But I can’t stop.

Xiao Wang didn't look at me today. I should say something to him, but I don't know what.

Maybe I’ll delete these words tomorrow. There’s no need to leave this behind.

But for now, I’ll let them stay here.

I told Meifang about it over dinner tonight.

Another formatting error cropped up in QA this morning. It wasn't a major issue, but I can't stand that kind of slackness when it comes to details. I was right there on the floor and called it out immediately; my voice might have been a bit loud. The subordinate looked pretty shaken, but I had to make it clear—details determine product quality, and product quality determines whether this company survives. I’m not exaggerating.

I told Meifang that I need to overhaul the department’s standard operating procedures. Just emphasizing it verbally isn't enough; it has to be documented with every step clearly defined. As she listened, she just looked at me that way, and I knew what she was thinking: *Here we go again.* But this time is different. I can feel that if things continue like this, the problems are only going to multiply.

She said, "Don't push yourself too hard." I didn't respond to that. After a few bites of food, I explained once more why these standards must be strictly enforced. She just nodded and kept eating.

The truth is, I know my subordinates are afraid of me. But what’s wrong with a little fear? Fear makes people diligent. I’ve been in this position for 12 years, and our defect rate is 25% lower than the industry average—that’s not because I have a pleasant temperament.

Lately, I just feel this constant urge to hurry. Whether it’s work or anything else. While I’m still able to move, I need to get everything done right.

original_messages.content:
Sunday, September 18, 2022, 10:47 PM

I haven’t slept well since getting back from the hospital yesterday. I just lay in bed, turning those numbers over and over in my head. 110, Grade 2, atherosclerosis. Meifang was sound asleep; I didn’t disturb her.

I went out this morning. I didn’t tell her where I was going. I bought a blood pressure monitor, a glucose meter, and a new notebook—black cover, high-quality paper. The cashier asked if I was buying them for a family member. I didn’t answer.

After getting home, I spent two hours in the workshop. I organized everything. I wiped all my tools clean. Then, I started recording.

8:15 AM: BP 128/82.
12:30 PM: BP 125/79.
3:45 PM: Blood sugar 5.8.
7:20 PM: BP 132/85.

I downloaded three apps: "BP Manager," "Health Log," and one specifically for tracking diet. The interfaces are all very clear. I entered everything I ate today—plain congee with pickles for breakfast, steamed fish and greens for lunch, tomato and egg noodles for dinner. No oil. No salt.

The doctor said I need long-term medication. But I’m thinking, what if I can keep these numbers within the normal range? If I stick to the logs, stick to the diet, and stick to the exercise—I’m going to walk 8,000 steps a day now, I will do it—then maybe I won’t have to take those pills? Or at least I can delay it?

Meifang asked why I was so busy today. I told her it was nothing, just that I wanted to be more meticulous about managing my health. She gave me a look... that kind of look, as if she already knew what was coming. I didn’t want to look her in the eye.

On the first page of the notebook, I wrote a title: "Health Management Plan: September 2022 – September 2023." Below it are weekly logs and monthly summaries. Everything is clear and orderly.

As long as I persist, as long as I don’t slack off, I can definitely reverse this. What the doctor said... maybe he just saw me at my worst moment. I’m starting now, starting today.

Continue tomorrow. The blood pressure monitor is on the nightstand.

I cannot slack off.

Meifang, I bought a blood pressure monitor and a glucose meter yesterday and already took my readings this morning. My blood pressure was 130/85, which is a bit better than what the doctor said. I plan to test twice a day—once in the morning and once at night—and keep a log in my notebook.

You need to be careful lately, too. I noticed you’ve been eating pickled vegetables again; those are no good for your blood pressure. We need to use less salt in our dinners—I’ll be keeping an eye on that. Also, I looked over your physical exam report, and your blood pressure is indeed on the high side. We can’t put this off anymore. I’m going with you to the hospital for a follow-up next week.

You don't have to believe everything the doctors say; some of their data might be off. I’m using an app to record everything now, so the data is more accurate. As long as we stay on top of managing it, it won't be that serious. I’ve already downloaded three apps that can track all our vitals.

Don’t worry, I have a plan. We just need to adjust our routine at home—we must be in bed by 11:00 PM and up by 6:00 AM. We’ll do this together.

Oh, and stop buying those greasy foods. We need to keep our diet a bit lighter for a while.

title: Reflections on Vulnerability and Cooperation in Health Management
content: On October 16, 2022, at 8:30 PM, the user reflected on a significant moment from earlier that day during a check-up at the hospital. After returning home, they sat in the study feeling at a loss for words. The doctor had given them positive news about their health, stating that the medication was effective and their heart rate was stabilizing. During the appointment, the user had intended to ask many questions but found themselves changing their approach when their wife, Meifang, sat beside them. They expressed a newfound sense of cooperation in their treatment, a departure from their usual mindset of strict control over their health and Meifang's well-being. The user acknowledged their past behavior of monitoring Meifang's health as if she were a metric to manage, realizing that this may have placed undue pressure on her. The doctor suggested they join a health management course, and instead of immediately declining due to work commitments, the user asked Meifang for her opinion. This shift in communication felt foreign yet significant. Meifang agreed to try the course, marking a decision that would foster their partnership in health. The user contemplated their vulnerability in admitting they cannot control everything and expressed gratitude towards Meifang for her support over the years. They discussed signing up for the course together that weekend, emphasizing their desire to make the most of their time together before retirement. The ordinary sounds of dinner preparation from the kitchen felt different that evening, symbolizing a shift in their relationship dynamics as they embraced a more cooperative approach to health management.

original_messages.content:
October 16, 2022, Evening

It’s been two hours since I got back from the hospital. Sitting here in the study, I still find myself somewhat at a loss for words.

The results from this morning’s check-up were steadier than expected. The doctor said the medication is working well and my heart rate is stabilizing. I had prepared a mountain of data and questions to ask, but with Meifang sitting beside me, I suddenly changed my mind. I heard myself say, "We are both cooperating with the treatment"—a strange choice of words coming from me. In the past, I would have said, "I am strictly managing it," or "I am controlling my diet." But today was different.

As I held my wife’s hand, I realized what I’ve been doing to her all these years. I’ve been "monitoring" her—monitoring her blood pressure, her diet, her physical exams. It was as if she were a quality control metric for me to manage. Yet she never once resisted. She was just there, by my side.

The doctor suggested joining a health management course. My first instinct was to refuse—too busy with work, not enough time. But I looked at Meifang and didn't say no right away. I asked her, "What do you think?" Those four words felt foreign coming out of my mouth. She said we could give it a try. And so, it was decided.

I wonder if this is what they call "vulnerability." Admitting that I can’t control everything, that I can’t stop my body from aging, and that I can’t ensure every plan stays on schedule. It’s not a comfortable feeling. But it’s not as terrifying as I imagined, either.

Perhaps all these years, I’ve been using perfect self-discipline to prove my worth. Now, I’m starting to wonder: was it worth it?

Meifang is downstairs preparing dinner. I can hear the sounds from the kitchen. It’s quiet, ordinary. But today, it sounds different.

I haven’t quite figured out what all of this means yet. But at the very least, I’m no longer in such a hurry.

Meifang, I wanted to say a few things to you.

I kept thinking about it yesterday at the hospital. All those years of "supervising" you—your diet, your checkups, your routine—I realize now that it probably put a lot of pressure on you. I thought I was taking care of you, but in reality, I was controlling you.

Yesterday, when you sat beside me and held my hand, you didn't let go the whole time the doctor was speaking. It was only then that I truly felt we aren't "supervisor and supervised." We are just... us. Together.

The doctor mentioned joining a health management course, and I want to go with you. Not so I can tell you what to do, but so we can learn together. To cooperate. I’ve never thought about that word in this way before.

I’ve seen how much you’ve put up with me all these years. I’m not very good at saying these things, but I want you to know—I’m grateful to you. Truly.

We still have time. Before I retire, while we can still do so many things together. I don't want to waste any more of it.

Shall we go sign up for that course together this weekend?

original_messages.content:
# Work Notebook

**Date: Wednesday, October 26, 2022**
**Location: Office**

---

## Thoughts on Technical Sharing

Had a brief chat with my supervisor this morning about my pre-retirement arrangements. He asked if I’d considered doing some training or a knowledge-sharing session for the younger engineers. I didn’t give him a direct answer at the time, but the idea has been on my mind ever since.

I used to feel this heavy obligation to "pass down" everything I’ve learned over the years in its entirety—as if that were the only way to prove these 40 years weren't for nothing. Looking back now, I think I was being too stubborn about it. Maybe that’s not what matters most.

**What I actually want to record:**

1. **On Quality Standards**
   - It’s not about pursuing perfection for perfection’s sake.
   - It’s about being accountable at every step and being responsible to the user.
   - The logic behind setting a standard is more important than the standard itself.
   - Example: Last year’s drop in defect rates wasn't due to new regulations, but because everyone finally understood the "why."

2. **On Process Improvement**
   - The goal of improvement isn't to make life difficult for people; it’s to make the work clearer.
   - Over the years, the proposals I made that actually worked were all rooted in real-world problems, not abstract imagination.
   - Listen to the voices on the front line; they know best where the bottlenecks are.

3. **On Working with People**
   - I need to be honest here: my approach has had its flaws.
   - Being blunt can be hurtful, and I know it has contributed to staff turnover.
   - Perhaps I should mention this in the session—not as self-criticism, but to tell the younger generation that being rigorous and being respectful are not mutually exclusive.
   - Where I fell short, they can do better.

4. **On Perseverance**
   - Spending 40 years in one place—some people say I lacked ambition.
   - But what I see is the value of deeply understanding an industry, a company, and a role.
   - Not all change is progress; sometimes, stability itself is a skill.

---

## Why I want to do this now

After that check-up with the doctor, things started to click. I can’t control aging, and I can’t ensure everything goes according to plan. What I can do, however, is record my reflections from all these years—not as a "legacy," but to clarify for myself what I’ve actually learned.

Meifang has been accompanying me on walks lately, and she mentioned I’ve become more talkative. I feel it too; I’m no longer in such a rush to prove anything.

If I do a session before I retire, this is what I want to talk about. It doesn't need to be formal—just a clear account of the experiences and the lessons. I want the younger ones to know there are different ways to do a job: you can be rigorous, but you can also be more human.

---

## To-Do

- Organize key improvement cases from the last 12 years (3-5 typical ones).
- Think about how to talk about the failed attempts.
- Confirm the specific timing and format of the session with my supervisor.
- Ask Hao and Yu what they think about me doing this.

To be honest, I felt a bit nervous when this idea first surfaced. Now that I’ve written it down, I actually feel a sense of relief.

# Work Log

**Date: Wednesday, October 26, 2022**
**Weather: Sunny**

---

This morning, I had a briefing with my supervisor to discuss the department's recent process optimization plans. As the meeting was drawing to a close, I brought up a new idea: I plan to host a "40 Years of Quality Management Experience" sharing session before I retire.

My supervisor listened intently. I laid out the concept clearly:

**Theme**: "From Frontline Inspector to Manager—Forty Years of Quality Management in Practice"

**Target Audience**: Mid-level management, key personnel from the Quality Control department, and interested technical staff.

**Core Modules**:
- The evolution and optimization of quality inspection processes
- Identification and solutions for common quality issues
- Balancing standardization and the human touch in team management
- Adaptation and innovation amidst industry shifts

He asked why I was proposing this now. I thought about it and told him the truth: "It’s not just about passing on knowledge. Everything I’ve learned over the years—if it just stays in my head, it’ll vanish once I retire. I want to document these things while I’m still on the job. It’s also a way for me to summarize and reflect on my own forty-year career."

He nodded and said it was a great idea, then asked me to put together an initial outline.

After returning to the office this afternoon, I jotted down a preliminary to-do list in my logbook:

- [ ] Compile department improvement cases from the past 12 years (data, results, lessons learned)
- [ ] Reflect on experiences from my time as a frontline inspector (comparisons with the present)
- [ ] Prepare detailed analyses for 3–5 typical case studies
- [ ] Reach out to potential participants (key subordinates, heads of other departments)
- [ ] Finalize the time and venue for the session
- [ ] Create the presentation outline and supporting materials

To be honest, I’ve been feeling anxious lately about the question, "What will I leave behind?" Now, I feel a bit more relaxed. Not everything has to be "passed down" to others. What matters more is that through this process, I can see clearly what I’ve done and what I’ve learned.

I mentioned this to Meifang during dinner. She was very supportive and even asked if I needed help organizing the materials. I said yes.

My physical condition has been okay these past two days after taking my medication. No particular discomfort. I’ll proceed with the scheduled medical checkup tomorrow.

---

- Communication with my supervisor went smoothly; no resistance encountered.
- This plan gives me a clearer sense of purpose, replacing vague anxiety with a concrete goal.

title: Reflections on Life, Control, and Connection: A Personal Journey
content: On October 30, 2022, at 8:00 PM, Chen Guilin sat in his study while his partner, Li Meifang, was already asleep. On his desk lay a cold cup of tea and today's medical report. He reflected on a profound statement he made earlier that day: 'Perhaps the meaning of life isn't in perfect control, but in genuine connection.' This realization surprised him, as it felt foreign yet resonated deeply with his thoughts. Over the past few days, since starting his medication, he noticed that the physical side effects were not as severe as he had anticipated, and he was beginning to relax. Unlike before, when he obsessively monitored his medical reports, he now approached them with a sense of acceptance. He recalled a moment from the previous night when Meifang held his hand for several seconds without speaking, a gesture he used to shy away from. This time, he embraced the connection, realizing how much he owed her for her patience and support throughout their thirty-five years together. He acknowledged that he had often disguised his need for control as responsibility, but Meifang had seen through it and remained by his side. Chen also reflected on a recent conversation with his friend Chen Hao, where instead of offering unsolicited advice about financial burdens, he simply listened and encouraged him to take his time. This shift in approach felt more authentic to him. He contemplated donating his precision tools to a technical school, recognizing that his initial motive of leaving a legacy was rooted in control. Now, he wanted to ensure that the tools would be used and appreciated by others. He felt a sense of lightness in letting go of control, which he had always feared would lead to panic. As he prepared for the upcoming work week, he planned to change his communication style with his subordinates, aiming to express high expectations positively. Chen Guilin concluded his reflections with a commitment to continue taking his medication, supporting Meifang, and cherishing the simple yet profound moments of connection they shared.

original_messages.content:
October 30, 2022, 8:00 PM

Li Meifang is already asleep. I’m sitting in the study; on the desk lies today’s medical report and a cup of tea that went cold long ago.

I said something to her today that left even me a bit stunned. I said, "Perhaps the meaning of life isn't in perfect control, but in genuine connection." Hearing those words come out of my mouth felt like someone was impersonating me. And yet, it really is what I was thinking.

Since I started the medication these past few days, the physical side effects haven't been as bad as I imagined. The doctor says it’s a good sign. But what’s stranger is that I’ve actually started to relax. I used to check my medical reports three times a day, recording every single number in a notebook, trying to force them back to "normal" through sheer willpower. Now... I still look at the reports, but I no longer feel the need to "subdue" them.

Last night, Meifang took my hand. She does this often, and I used to pull away after a moment to get back to my accounts or the news. But this time, I didn't. I let her hold it—maybe for five or six seconds. She didn’t say anything, and neither did I. We just held hands. Eventually, she let go gently and went to the kitchen to pour me some water.

I realize now that I owe her a great deal. For thirty-five years, I’ve used excuses like "monitoring her blood pressure" or "managing the family finances" to package my need for control as "responsibility." In truth, it was just my way of proving I was useful, that I deserved to be needed—by controlling everything. She saw through it long ago, but she never said a word. She just stayed by my side, waiting.

Chen Hao called recently saying his mortgage is a heavy burden. In the past, I would have immediately started analyzing his finances, giving him advice, even feeling a bit dissatisfied with his "poor planning." This time, I just listened, then told him, "It’s okay, take your time." There was a pause on the other end of the line; he didn’t seem used to me responding like that. I’m not used to it either. But it felt... more real.

Then there’s that idea about donating my tools to the technical school. Initially, I thought of it as "legacy"—wanting young people to learn what I’ve accumulated over forty years. But today I realized that was just another form of control; I wanted their learning to prove that my value wouldn't vanish with retirement. I still want to donate them, but the reason has changed. I just want to put those tools where they can continue to be used and cherished. As for who uses them or what they learn, that’s not for me to decide, nor does it need to be.

It’s strange. I always thought letting go of control would make me panic. But actually, it makes me feel... light?

My subordinates at the office are still a bit afraid of me. I know that. But lately, I’ve been thinking that maybe I could try a different way. Not by lowering standards, but... by changing how I communicate. Letting them know my expectations are high because I believe they can do well, not because I’m disappointed in them. This will require me to say more, and I’ve never been good at that. But perhaps it’s worth learning.

Tomorrow is Monday. Another week begins. I’ll keep taking the medicine, keep working, and keep being there for Meifang. And maybe, at the right moment, I’ll sit with her—saying nothing, just holding her hand.

That is enough.

# Work Log: October 30, 2022

**Sunday, 20:00**

I’ve been reflecting on something over the past few days. This afternoon, while sitting with Meifang for a long time, she mentioned that I’ve been talking a bit more lately. I just smiled and didn’t deny it.

Last Friday’s medical report showed that things have stabilized. The doctor said to just keep taking the medication on schedule and come in for regular check-ups. Meifang was right there beside me taking notes, even more focused than I was. It made me think back on all the "supervising" I’ve done at home over the years—checking her blood pressure, monitoring her diet. My intentions might have been right, but my approach was probably too rigid. She never complained; instead, she’s now taking the initiative to accompany me to the hospital. It’s a strange feeling, but a grounding one.

Back to the office tomorrow. I’ve been thinking about how to organize everything I’ve accumulated over these forty years before I retire. It’s not necessarily about passing it on to someone specific, but I feel there should be a record. On Monday, I plan to talk to my supervisor about putting together a summary of my quality management experience in the first half of next year, perhaps as a formal document. Also, regarding that technical school—I want to move forward with that. I plan to systematically categorize and label the precision tools in the workshop and donate them. In my hands, they are just tools; in the hands of students, they might become something more.

Feedback from my subordinates has been better lately. I’ve noticed that when giving feedback, I’ve started asking for their thoughts first instead of just pointing out problems. The defect rate remains low, but the atmosphere seems less tense. I haven't fully processed this shift myself, but it feels right.

Haohao called last week saying his mortgage pressure is still quite heavy. I didn’t jump in with advice immediately; instead, I asked what his plans were. He said he might need to adjust his work schedule. I told him, "As long as you’ve thought it through. Let us know if you need help." I surprised myself a bit saying that, but in that moment, I was being sincere.

Yuyu’s work in Guangzhou is also going well. She said she wants to come back for a visit after National Day; Meifang and I are both very happy about it.

Perhaps the meaning of life isn't about perfect control, but about genuine connection. That thought surfaced while I was chatting with Meifang—I didn't expect to say it myself. But once it was out there, it felt like I had finally admitted something.

Onward to next week.

---
*Recorded by: Chen Guilin*  
*Date: October 30, 2022*

# MEMO

**Date**: July 5, 2023, 7:00 PM
**Subject**: Reflections on the Passing of Values

---

I was on the phone with my daughter today when a thought suddenly struck me.

She was talking about student development, and I was listening. Then I realized—what she is pursuing seems to be the exact same thing I pursue in the factory.

I have always strived for product excellence. She strives for the growth of her students. My son upholds integrity in real estate sales.

On the surface, these paths look different. But at their core, we are all chasing "excellence."

Or rather, we are all striving to do things well. To do things right.

It’s a strange realization. I’ve never thought about it this way before. I used to think the value of my work existed only within the factory walls. Now it seems that this obsession with excellence is alive in them, just in different forms.

It’s not that I preached any grand philosophies to them. It’s that they saw how I worked. And now, they are pursuing that same thing in their own way.

This makes me feel that perhaps my value won’t simply vanish when I leave the factory. It already exists elsewhere, in other forms, continuing on.

The thought brings me a sense of peace.

---

**Postscript**:
The tool donation doesn’t seem like an empty gesture now. Perhaps that, too, is a way of passing it on—passing the pursuit of excellence to more people.

I need to think on this further.

Yu came back today. We talked about her curriculum design; she did a great job.

She said she strives for excellence in her teaching, just like the standards I hold in my quality control work. I didn't realize she felt that way.

We are both pursuing the same thing, just in different ways.

Thinking about it this way makes me feel a bit more at ease.

July 7, 2023, 9:00 PM

The only light in the study comes from the desk lamp. My wife went to bed a while ago; it’s quiet downstairs.

Insomnia again tonight, but this time it’s different. It’s not the restless, agitated kind where you toss and turn. It’s... how should I put it? I’m captivated by something. I don’t want to go to sleep.

While I was tidying up my tools this afternoon, that quality crisis from 2010 suddenly crossed my mind. Remember that? The supplier cut corners, our inspectors missed it, and it nearly ruined the company’s reputation. I wrote the entire improvement plan back then—from source inspection and mid-process sampling to final acceptance. I added double-checks to every single step. Later, that system was adopted across the whole industry.

I sat down at my desk and started writing it all down. Not for anyone in particular—to be honest, I don’t know who would even read it. I just felt like these things shouldn't be allowed to simply vanish. Those experiences, those lessons—they deserve to be recorded.

As I wrote, I found myself asking strange questions. For instance: why did I think of that solution back then? What was it that kept me going until the plan was finished? I was only in my fifties then; I was still working, and I had clear goals. What about now?

But tonight is different. When I got to that case study, it suddenly hit me—maybe I could organize all of this into a proper document. Nothing fancy, just a clear explanation: when you face a problem like this, here is how you should think, and here is what you should do. For the young people. For the inspectors who just started at the factory.

I put down my pen and stared at the ceiling for a while.

The idea makes me feel... what’s the word? Fulfilled? It’s not the satisfaction you get from finishing a job; it’s something else. It feels like I’m doing something meaningful, but it’s no longer for a promotion or a year-end review. It’s just... a pure desire to pass on what I know.

It’s almost 11:00 PM now. I should be tired, but I want to keep writing. I want to record that process optimization from 2015. I want to include the failed attempts, too—those are just as important.

My wife is asleep upstairs. Her blood pressure has been a bit high lately; I need to remind her to take her medicine tomorrow. But for now, I want to stay right here.

There are still many blank pages in the notebook under the lamp.

I want to fill them.

Meifang, go ahead and get some sleep. I’m going to stay in the study and write for a bit longer.

I went through those quality inspection materials today and wanted to jot down the key processes and experiences. I’ve been writing until now, and it feels quite productive. Some things that weren't clear to me before have finally started to make sense now that I'm putting them on paper.

Don't wait up for me. Remember to take your blood pressure medicine. I’ll make some soup for you tomorrow morning.

original_messages.content:
# Diary

July 14, 2023, Evening

After the game ended, my chess partner, A, asked me: "You’ve changed lately. You used to only care about the game itself, but now, you’re telling stories."

I didn’t answer right away. I thought about it for a long time while packing up the chess pieces.

Maybe he’s right. I am changing. But as for when this change began, I can’t quite say for sure.

Perhaps it was those numbers on my last medical report. Or the stress in Hao’s voice when we spoke on the phone in Shenzhen a while back. Or maybe it was Meifang’s blood pressure rising again recently; sitting beside her, I suddenly realized we’ve lived like this for 35 years, yet we’ve never truly had a real conversation.

A asked, "Want to go for a small get-together in the suburbs? Just a few of us, nothing formal, just sitting around."

My first instinct was to refuse. I never participate in these kinds of things. But this time, I paused. I looked at his face and remembered that we’ve been playing chess here every week for years, yet we’ve never actually spent time together away from the board.

I said, "Okay."

The moment I said that word, I felt something. It wasn't excitement, but a strange sense of relief.

I have always been in control. Controlling every detail of my work, every entry in the accounts, and the distance between me and my family—maintaining my independence under the guise of "caring." I thought that was what it meant to be responsible.

But lately, I’ve begun to understand that I cannot control everything. I can’t control Hao’s mortgage, I can’t control Meifang’s blood pressure, and I can’t control the fluctuations of the indicators in my own body. I can’t even control how my days after retirement should be spent.

But I can choose. I can choose how to live.

The tools should be donated to the school. I should go ahead with the lectures, too. Not to leave behind some kind of "legacy"—that word sounds too heavy now. I just want to pass these things, these experiences, along in a different way. Just as my daughter teaches students in her classroom and my son builds houses in Shenzhen. We are each doing our own part.

The travel plans with Meifang need to be taken seriously as well. Not as a routine obligation, but because I truly want to go and see the world with her.

Writing these things in a diary feels a bit foreign. Usually, I only keep work logs, records of accounts, and things that can be quantified. Now, I am writing about feelings.

A looked at me as if waiting for me to say more. I didn't. But I think maybe at the next gathering, I will speak a bit more.

Not for anyone else to hear. Just because, perhaps, it is finally time.

Meifang, while I was playing chess at the club today, my friends all mentioned that I’ve seemed different lately. I didn't pay much attention to it at the time, but thinking back on it now, I feel they were right.

I told them about giving the lecture at the school and my plan to organize those tools to donate. One of them, Old Jia, said it sounds like I’m doing something truly meaningful. I didn't explain much, but I did feel a sense of peace in my heart.

Later, they invited us to a get-together—not just for chess, but with our families too. I hesitated for a moment, but I said yes. I was wondering, maybe you could come along? I know this isn't exactly your kind of social scene, but I’d like you to meet the people who have kept me company over the years; they’re actually quite decent folks.

I’ve noticed all the support you’ve given me lately. You never complained about me being quiet, and you never gave me the cold shoulder because of my temper. Do you remember what you said a while back? "You’re finally starting to figure things out." I’ve kept those words with me ever since.

As for our travel plans, I’ve scouted out a few places. If you have time this weekend, let’s sit down and talk about where you’d like to go. I want this trip to be something we decide on together, not just me planning it on my own.

I’ll tell you more about today when I get home tonight.
